newsitem.title: GERMANY: German farmers aim for separate gene maize sowings.
newsitem.headline: German farmers aim for separate gene maize sowings.

text.p: German farm union (DBV) is aiming to ensure there will be separate planting of genetically-modified maize, which is expected to be given approval for cultivation in Europe, a spokesman said on Tuesday.
"It's early days but we're talking to plant breeders and the food industry about the separate sowing, storage and processing of such maize," a DBV spokesman said.
"We're not against biotechnology but we have to bear the consumer reaction in mind...perhaps we can even help to show the advantages of gene-modified crops in that way," he said.
He did not expect German farmers to be offered the new type of seeds for 1997 spring plantings and autumn harvests, but believed it likely that gene maize may be sown in 1998.

The EU Commission on December 18 approved transgenic maize, developed by Swiss chemical firm Ciba Geigy AG and grown in the U.S., for import and sale in the EU -- against opposition from environmental group Greenpeace and others.
The Ciba maize, which so far makes up an estimated 0.6 percent of the 1996/97 U.S. corn crop, has been made resistant to the herbicide glufosinate and the corn-borer pest.
Greenpeace says the new maize, through the insertion of an antibiotic "marker gene," may increase human and animal resistance to the healing effects of antibiotics.
A spokeswoman at the organisation's office in Hamburg said campaigners would try to put pressure on the European Parliament, which has to endorse the decision in mid-January.
Greenpeace would also keep up a fight against gene-altered U.S. soybeans, where it sees unknown health risks.
It would soon present an EU-wide study documenting consumer opposition to the genetic modification of food products.
It would also keep a watchful eye on the implementation of labelling rules under the EU novel food law, which may come too late to include the now approved gene soya and maize products.
Economist Klaus Schumacher of Toepfer International said U.S. gene maize would mostly be bought by Spain and Portugal. Transport from there to other EU countries was unprofitable.
The two take about 2.0-2.5 million tonnes of annual imports from the U.S. and the rest of the EU roughly 500,000 or 600,000 tonnes, of which some material is later re-exported, he said.
Dutch and Belgian starch industries process imported maize, often for the re-export of starch products to third countries.
Germany uses two thirds of its own 2.6 million tonne maize crop in feed and imports 900,000 tonnes, mainly from France, which is mostly for industrial use.
